deep.reconstruction:
This page has no mathematics: no formulas, derivations or computations. It is introductory methodological prose from Riemann's unfinished essay on the mechanics of the ear. Henle published it posthumously in 1867 as 'Mechanik des Ohres' in the Zeitschrift für rationelle Medicin, and it is reprinted in Riemann's Gesammelte Werke.

Content of the page, in order:
(1) The previous page said Riemann assumes the physiological facts of hearing are known, citing Helmholtz's 'Lehre von den Tonempfindungen'. Here he likewise assumes the anatomy of the ear is known. He asks the reader to consult an illustrated anatomy handbook if needed.
(2) For the newest findings on the cochlea and the ear in general, he refers to the recently issued third instalment ('dritte Lieferung') of the second volume of Henle's 'Handbuch der (systematischen) Anatomie des Menschen'. That is the Eingeweidelehre volume, whose sense-organ part appeared c. 1866. This dates the page to about 1866.
(3) He states his sole task: to explain the physiological facts of hearing from these anatomical facts.
(4) He names the relevant parts of the ear: the tympanic cavity (Paukenhöhle) and the labyrinth, which consists of the vestibule, the semicircular canals and the cochlea.
(5) He announces a two-stage method, which runs onto the next page. First, infer from the structure of each part what it might contribute to the ear's performance. Then, for each part, start from the task it must solve and derive the conditions needed for a satisfactory solution. This is his 'inverse' methodology: deduce necessary mechanical conditions from observed function.

Why the method matters: on the next page it is applied to the tympanic apparatus. There, faithful transmission of timbre ('Klang') requires that air-pressure changes be passed to the labyrinth fluid amplified by a constant ratio at every instant, i.e. a linear, distortion-free transmission. This is set against Helmholtz's theory of the ear's motions.

results.what: Methodological programme: infer the function of each part of the ear from its anatomy, then derive necessary mechanical conditions from the task each part must perform (the analytic/'inverse' method of Mechanik des Ohres).
results.modern_name: Functional / inverse-problem approach in auditory biomechanics (middle ear as impedance-matching, linear pressure transformer)
results.usually_credited_to: Riemann's own posthumous essay 'Mechanik des Ohres' (1867); the middle-ear pressure-amplification idea goes back to Helmholtz (1868, 'Die Mechanik der Gehörknöchelchen') and earlier anatomists

deep.surprise_reason: The page is purely introductory prose (literature references and a statement of method) from Riemann's known, published posthumous essay 'Mechanik des Ohres'. It contains no mathematics and nothing that is not already in the printed text.
transcription_corrections: The machine transcription matches the image well.
The interlinear insertions are correctly placed: 'der' is written above, before 'Anatomie' ('Handbuch der Anatomie'), and 'zu' is written above, between 'Hülfe' and 'nehmen' ('zur Hülfe zu nehmen').
The marginal number '13' (folio number, beside the line '...zur Hülfe zu nehmen') and the page number '9' (top right) are archival and authorial pagination respectively, not part of the text.
'Henles Handbuch der Anatomie des Menschen' refers to J. Henle, Handbuch der systematischen Anatomie des Menschen, Bd. II (Eingeweidelehre), 3. Lieferung.
